skill_drafts.name: Column selector execution with qsv select
skill_drafts.description: Use qsv select selector syntax to choose, order, or duplicate columns by index, header name, range, last-column token, or regex when a delimited file needs a precise column subset without changing row data.
skill_drafts.objective: Produce a delimited output with the requested columns selected and ordered from an input delimited file, without changing row data.
applicable_signals: Caller knows target columns by index, header name, range, last-column token, or regex
Requested change is limited to column projection, ordering, or duplication
Input is a delimited file with usable headers for name-based or regex selectors
contraindications: Need to filter rows or transform cell values
Need to join or aggregate datasets
Column names are unknown and cannot be inferred from input headers
Need a privacy-specific deletion policy or column-level randomization as the primary procedure
intervention_moves: Map requested columns to qsv select selector syntax
Use 1-based indices, ranges, and header-name ranges
Use _ for the last column and /regex/ for pattern-based selection
Quote column names or selectors that conflict with selector syntax
Execute qsv select and verify output column set and order
workflow_steps: Confirm which columns are requested and whether selection will use indices, header names, ranges, the last-column token _, or regex.
Construct the selector using 1-based indices, ranges, header-name ranges, _ for the last column, and /regex/ for pattern matches.
Repeat selectors to duplicate columns or reorder output arbitrarily.
Quote header names or selectors that conflict with selector syntax or shell metacharacters.
Run qsv select with the selector and input file.
Inspect the output to confirm exactly the requested columns appear in the requested order and row data is unchanged.
triggers: Need to select columns by header name, range, regex, or last column
Need to duplicate or reorder selected columns
CSV or delimited column projection is required without row filtering
constraints: Assumes a delimited input with stable column order for index-based selectors and accessible header names for name-based or regex selectors.
Selector syntax is 1-based and order-preserving by default; repeated columns are allowed.
The output must preserve all row values; only columns are projected, reordered, or duplicated.
Resolve missing or ambiguous target columns before execution instead of guessing.
cautions: Regex selectors can match unintended columns; verify the output column set.
Header-name ranges depend on current header ordering and may shift if upstream columns change.
Do not use --random for this skill's deterministic selector-based output contract.
This skill does not define row filtering, value transforms, joins, or aggregations.
output_contract: A CSV output containing exactly the specified columns in the specified order, with row data otherwise unchanged. If the selector cannot be resolved, no valid column projection is produced.

examples.input: Select the first and fourth columns
Select the first 4 columns by name

examples.notes: Uses a regex selector against header names.

metadata.prompt: Construct a qsv select selector from the caller's requested columns. Use 1-based indices (e.g., 1,4), ranges (1-4, 3-), header-name ranges (Header1-Header4), _ for the last column, and /regex/ for pattern matches. Repeat selectors to duplicate columns. Quote header names that conflict with selector syntax. Run qsv select with the selector and input file, then verify the output header has exactly the requested columns in the requested order and that row data is unchanged. If target columns cannot be resolved, do not guess; report the ambiguity.

skill_drafts.name: Sensitive column removal with negated regex selection
skill_drafts.description: Use qsv select with a negated regex selector to drop columns whose names match sensitive identifiers such as SSN, account number, or password before sharing or exporting data. Invoke when column headers reliably indicate PII or credentials and the output CSV will leave the current trust boundary.
skill_drafts.objective: Prevent disclosure of sensitive columns by excluding them from the selected output.
applicable_signals: Dataset contains known sensitive column names
Output CSV will be shared, published, or sent downstream
Column headers reliably indicate PII or credentials
The goal is exclusion of named columns rather than general column reordering or inspection
contraindications: Sensitive columns are not known and cannot be pattern-matched
Data must retain all columns for internal analysis
Column names are misleading or absent
The sensitive data may live under innocuous column names that the regex cannot detect
intervention_moves: Enumerate the sensitive column names or a regex pattern that matches them
Build a negated regex selector in the form !/pattern/ that matches only those sensitive names
Run qsv select with that selector on the input CSV
Verify the resulting header omits every matching column and preserves the remaining columns
Hand off the redacted CSV to the downstream sharing or export step
workflow_steps: Identify the sensitive column names or a regex pattern that matches them, for example SSN, account_no, and password.
Construct a single negated regex selector that matches those names, such as !/SSN|account_no|password/.
Run qsv select with the negated selector against the input CSV, single-quoting the selector to protect it from shell interpretation.
Inspect the output header: confirm no column matching the sensitive regex remains, and confirm that expected non-sensitive columns are still present.
Proceed with sharing, publishing, or exporting the redacted CSV only after the header check passes.
triggers: A CSV will be shared, published, or sent to a downstream system
Column headers contain known sensitive identifiers such as SSN, account_no, password, or similar PII/credential labels
A pattern can be written that matches the sensitive column names to be removed
A privacy or compliance review requires excluding named sensitive columns from the exported file
constraints: The selector must be a negated regex (!/pattern/) so non-matching columns are retained and matching columns are dropped.
The regex is evaluated against column names, not cell values; it cannot detect sensitive content stored under unrelated headers.
The selector should be single-quoted when passed through a shell so the pipe characters and other special characters are not interpreted by the shell.
Verification of the emitted header is required before the output leaves the trust boundary.
This guardrail operates on column names; it must not be treated as a substitute for content-level inspection when headers are unreliable.
cautions: A negated regex drops only columns whose names match the pattern; misnamed, missing, or newly added sensitive columns will pass through unnoticed.
If the pattern is too broad, legitimate columns may be dropped; if too narrow, sensitive columns may remain.
Column names that look similar to sensitive identifiers can cause unintended removal, so the header check must confirm both exclusions and retentions.
This move reduces disclosure risk for known named columns but does not guarantee full de-identification of the dataset.
output_contract: A CSV whose header omits every column matching the sensitive-name regex while preserving all non-matching columns in their original order, plus confirmation that the emitted header was checked before the file is shared, published, or sent downstream.

examples.input: A CSV with columns including SSN, account_no, and password that is about to be shared externally.
examples.notes: The negated regex drops the three named sensitive columns and retains the rest; single quotes protect the selector from shell interpretation.

examples.input: A CSV that must be checked after redaction before export.
examples.output: Run the negated-regex selection, then inspect the output header to confirm no SSN, account_no, or password column remains.
examples.notes: Verification is part of the guardrail, not an optional extra step.

metadata.prompt: Given a CSV whose output will be shared, published, or sent downstream, identify the column names or name patterns that must not be disclosed, then run qsv select with a single negated regex selector listing those identifiers (for example: qsv select '!/SSN|account_no|password/' input.csv). The negated selector retains every column that does not match and drops every column that does. Single-quote the selector so the shell does not expand or split it. After running, inspect the emitted header to confirm no matching column remains and that all expected non-sensitive columns are still present before handing the output to the next step.

skill_drafts.name: Column order sorting and seeded randomization
skill_drafts.description: Apply qsv select --sort to order selected columns lexicographically by byte value, or --random with an optional --seed to reproducibly shuffle already-selected columns. Use when column membership is already determined and only column order needs deterministic or reproducible pseudo-random control.
skill_drafts.objective: Reorder selected columns deterministically or pseudo-randomly while preserving row data.
applicable_signals: Column selection is complete but order is inconsistent
A deterministic column order is needed for comparison
A reproducible shuffled column order is needed for testing or masking
contraindications: Need to shuffle rows rather than columns
Need to modify cell values or headers
Randomization without a seed is required for cryptographic purposes
intervention_moves: Use --sort to order selected columns lexicographically by byte value
Use --random --seed <value> to produce the same shuffled column order across runs
Combine --sort or --random with existing selector syntax such as 1-, 1,4,5-7
workflow_steps: Confirm the column selection expression is already defined.
Choose --sort for lexicographic byte-order and deterministic output.
Or choose --random for pseudo-random column order.
If reproducibility is required, add --seed with a fixed value.
Run qsv select with the selector plus the ordering flag and pass the resulting CSV to downstream processing.
triggers: Need a consistent column order for downstream comparison
Need reproducible randomized column order for testing or masking
Columns have already been selected and only order should change
constraints: Only column order should change; selected columns and row data must be preserved.
--random without a seed is not reproducible.
--sort orders columns lexicographically by byte value.
cautions: Seeded randomization is reproducibility-oriented, not cryptographic.
Use column ordering flags on top of an explicit selection expression rather than as a substitute for selecting columns.
output_contract: Output CSV has the same selected columns rearranged by lexicographic order or by a seeded random order.

examples.notes: Orders all selected columns by byte value.

examples.input: Reproducibly shuffle columns with a seed
examples.notes: Uses a seed so the shuffled column order can be repeated.

examples.input: Select a subset and then shuffle with a seed
examples.notes: Applies ordering flags after the selector expression.

metadata.prompt: After selecting the desired columns, add --sort to order them lexicographically by byte value, or add --random (optionally with --seed <value>) to shuffle column order. Preserve row data and selected column membership; only column order should change.
